digital-risk-protection.title: Brand impersonation and takedowns
digital-risk-protection.summary: Someone sets up a fake sign-in page using your company’s name. The team needs to confirm the impersonation, get the right person to authorize a removal request, and check whether the page comes down.
digital-risk-protection.owner: Brand protection or the security operations team investigates. Legal or the trademark owner may need to authorize the request.
digital-risk-protection.question: Walk me through the last fake site. Who confirmed it was yours to report, and who checked that customers could no longer reach it?
digital-risk-protection.measure: Track time to confirm an impersonation, time to submit an authorized request, and time to independently confirm removal.

options.ask: What proof of trademark authority do we need before you can act?
Which kinds of brand abuse qualify for a takedown under our agreement?
How do we distinguish a submitted request from a confirmed removal?
How do you distinguish a submitted takedown request from a site that is confirmed offline?

itdr.title: Stolen employee credentials
itdr.summary: An employee’s work email shows up in breach data or a report of stolen credentials. The first decision is whether the finding involves a current work account and what the identity team should do about it.
itdr.owner: Threat intelligence or the SOC triages the finding. Identity operations checks account status and recent activity, then records the response.
itdr.question: When a vendor reports an employee login, what evidence lets you distinguish a current work account from an old account at another service?
itdr.measure: Track time to an account match and the percentage of confirmed matches with a documented response. Count evidence of actual account use separately.

options.ask: Can we see which breached service and customer identifier produced the match?
What source context accompanies the alert, and where does the identity team confirm whether the account was used?
Which verified identifier matched the record, and how do we connect it to a current identity or device?

cspm.title: Public cloud storage exposure
cspm.summary: A storage bucket or container appears to be public. Cloud security needs to determine who can read it, whether sharing was intentional, and which team owns the setting.
cspm.owner: Cloud security reviews the access finding. The application or data owner confirms the intended audience and approves any permission change.
cspm.question: Can you show the permission that allowed access, identify who approved the sharing, and show that the corrected policy took effect?
cspm.measure: Track time to identify the owner and verify the intended access. Use separate evidence when investigating whether anyone actually downloaded data.

options.ask: Which policy grants access to anyone, and which grants access only to a named AWS account?
Can we distinguish an internet-reachable Azure storage account from a container that allows anonymous reads?
Which bucket was identified, and who can authorize a playbook to change its access?
